lessons.title: Coastal Management & a Distinctive UK Coastline

before.content_html:
Why People Want to Defend the Coast

Around 17 million people in the UK live within 10 km of the coast. They have homes, businesses, ports and farmland to lose. Where coastal erosion eats into the land at speed — or where storm flooding threatens low-lying ground — communities demand defence. The challenge is that defending one stretch of coast often damages another, and the cheapest defences are not always the best. Hard engineering tries to stop the sea. Soft engineering tries to work with it.

Hard Engineering: Big, Visible, Expensive

A sea wall is a concrete or stone barrier that reflects waves. It defends towns well — the curved sea wall at Blackpool has protected the promenade since the 1920s — but it costs around £6,000 per metre, and reflected waves can scour the beach below. Groynes are wooden or stone fences built out into the sea; they trap sediment moving by longshore drift, fattening the beach. The downside is that beaches downdrift are starved of sand, sometimes accelerating erosion further along the coast. Rip rap (large boulders piled at the cliff foot) absorbs wave energy cheaply but looks unsightly and can become unstable in storms.

Key Fact

Hard engineering protects what it shields but often shifts the problem along the coast. Soft engineering accepts coastal change and works with it — usually cheaper but slower-acting.

Soft Engineering: Working With the Sea

Beach nourishment involves pumping sand from offshore onto an eroding beach, restoring it as a natural buffer. It looks invisible once finished and protects the cliff behind, but the sand erodes over time and must be topped up every few years. Lincolnshire’s coast is renourished annually at a cost of around £7 million. Managed retreat is more radical: defences are deliberately removed or breached, allowing the sea to flood low-value land such as farmland or marsh. Salt marshes form in the new intertidal zone, absorbing storm energy and creating wildlife habitat. The Medmerry scheme in West Sussex (2013) is the largest UK example to date.

A Distinctive UK Coastline: The Holderness Coast

The 61 km Holderness coast in East Yorkshire, between Flamborough Head and Spurn Head, is one of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe. It is made of boulder clay — a soft, unconsolidated material left behind by glaciers around 18,000 years ago. The cliffs retreat by about 1.5–2 metres each year on average, and individual storms can take 5 metres in a single week.

Why so fast? Three reasons: the rock is soft and slumps when wet; the long fetch across the North Sea generates powerful destructive waves; and the prevailing easterly storms hit the cliff at an angle that drives strong longshore drift south. Material eroded from the cliffs at Mappleton or Hornsea is carried south to feed the sand spit at Spurn Head.

In 1991 the village of Mappleton received a £2 million scheme of two large rock groynes plus rip rap. The defences saved 30 homes and the cliff-top road. But by trapping longshore-drift sediment, the groynes starved the coast immediately to the south. At Cowden, just 3 km down the coast, erosion accelerated to 10 metres a year. Farmland and a caravan site there have been lost. The Mappleton case is a textbook reminder that coastal defences shift the problem — they rarely solve it.

How Holderness Has Changed Over Time

Roman maps suggest the coast was 4 km further east 2,000 years ago. Some 30 villages have been lost to the sea since the Domesday Book in 1086, including Ravenser Odd — once a major port. Today, places like Skipsea and Hornsea are partially defended; others such as Aldbrough are not. Climate change adds pressure: rising sea levels mean higher base water levels for storms, and more frequent winter storms mean more cliff failures per year. Local councils now use a shoreline management plan that decides for each stretch whether to ‘hold the line’, ‘advance the line’, ‘manage realignment’ or ‘take no active intervention’.

Residents whose homes are at risk want defences. Farmers losing fields want compensation if the policy is to retreat. Environmental groups support managed retreat because salt marshes are valuable habitats. Engineers worry about the engineering integrity of older sea walls. Government agencies (the Environment Agency in England) have to balance cost-benefit: defences are usually only funded where the value of property at risk exceeds the build and maintenance cost. That means low-value farmland is often allowed to flood while towns are protected.

Key Fact

Holderness erodes at 1.5–2 m/year because boulder clay is soft, fetch is long across the North Sea, and waves arrive at an angle that drives strong longshore drift southwards.

practice_questions.text: Which is an example of soft engineering?
practice_questions.marks: A. Sea wall  |  B. Rip rap  |  C. Beach nourishment (correct)  |  D. Groynes — 1 mark for C.

Mastering: A coastal management approach where defences are removed or breached so the sea can flood low-value land, often creating salt marsh. Secure: Allowing the sea to flood low-value land deliberately. Developing: Letting the coast flood. Emerging: Vague reference to flooding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why hard engineering at one location can increase erosion further along the coast.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Groynes/sea walls trap or reflect sediment, so longshore drift carries less sand to coastlines downdrift; without that natural buffer, those coasts are exposed and erosion accelerates. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions sediment without process. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location of one named UK coastline that is rapidly eroding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names Holderness, places it East Yorkshire between Flamborough Head and Spurn Head, gives a length (~61 km) and an erosion rate (1.5–2 m/yr). Secure: Three of the above. Developing: Names the coast with one detail. Emerging: General reference only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Holderness coast erodes so quickly.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (soft boulder clay; long North Sea fetch generating destructive waves; prevailing easterly storms driving longshore drift) with reference to specific places (Mappleton, Hornsea). Secure: Two reasons with example. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Lists factors without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of using hard engineering to defend a UK coastline you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing benefits (protection of property, jobs) against costs (downdrift erosion, expense, visual impact), grounded in a named UK case study with figures, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial analysis. Emerging: One side only.

before.exam_tip_html: Edexcel rewards balanced answers on coastal management. For 8-mark ‘assess’ questions, give at least one hard engineering and one soft engineering example, name the UK location, give a cost or rate where you can (groynes ≈ £5,000–10,000/m; Holderness retreat ≈ 2 m/year), and finish with a justified judgement. Avoid “defences are good because they protect homes” — always include the trade-off.

lessons.title: River Management & a Distinctive UK River

before.content_html:
Why Rivers Flood

A flood happens when the volume of water in a river exceeds the capacity of its channel. Both natural and human factors push rivers over the edge. Natural causes include heavy or prolonged rainfall, snowmelt on saturated ground, low-permeability rocks like clay that send water straight into the river, and steep upland slopes that speed runoff. Human causes include urbanisation (concrete prevents infiltration), deforestation (no roots to soak up water), and agriculture (compacted soil and field drains). All of these shorten lag time on the hydrograph — meaning the river peaks faster after a storm.

Key Fact

UK flooding is rarely one cause. Major events combine prolonged frontal rainfall, saturated catchments, urban runoff and historical changes to land use. Always discuss multiple causes in extended writing.

Hard Engineering: Containing the River

Hard engineering tries to contain or speed up the river. Dams and reservoirs store flood water and release it slowly, also providing drinking water and hydropower. The Kielder dam in Northumberland holds 200 million cubic metres of water but cost £167 million in the 1980s and drowned a Northumbrian valley. Channelisation — straightening and widening a river so flood water flows away faster — works for the protected stretch but pushes higher peaks downstream and damages river ecology by removing riffles, pools and bankside habitat. Even simple flood walls count as hard engineering: the Thames Barrier (1982) protects central London from tidal surge floods, and the Foss Barrier in York holds back surge water from the Ouse during winter floods.

Soft Engineering: Working With the Catchment

Soft engineering takes a different approach — it works with the catchment rather than fighting it. Floodplain zoning uses land-use planning instead of concrete: fields and parks beside the river are accepted as places where water will spread; housing and infrastructure are kept on higher ground. Washlands are deliberately maintained low areas next to the river that flood naturally, like the Ouse Washes in East Anglia where 24 km2 of farmland take up flood water in winter. River restoration removes old channelisation, allowing rivers to meander again. The River Skerne in Darlington was famously re-meandered in the 1990s; flood peaks downstream fell measurably and wildlife returned. Combined with upland peat rewetting in the Pennines and tree planting in upper catchments, soft engineering is increasingly the preferred long-term strategy.

A Distinctive UK River: The River Tees

The River Tees flows 137 km from Cross Fell in the North Pennines to the North Sea at Middlesbrough. Its journey runs through every classic landform. In the upper course at High Force, the river drops 22 metres over a layer of hard whinstone capping softer carboniferous limestone, retreating slowly upstream and leaving a steep wooded gorge. The middle course swings through a wide-floored valley with classic meanders near Yarm. The lower course flows across a broad floodplain to a large tidal estuary at Teesside.

Human activity has reshaped the Tees throughout its course. Cow Green Reservoir (built 1970) regulates flow upstream. Channel improvements at Yarm and a flood-relief storage area at Hurworth Burn protect riverside towns. The estuary has been heavily industrialised since the 1850s — reclaimed for steelworks, chemical plants and the modern port — reducing the natural mudflats and salt marsh that once buffered storm surges.

Storm Arwen in November 2021 and Storm Babet in October 2023 brought serious flooding to towns along the Tees including Yarm and Stockton. Even with reservoirs and channelisation, the lower Tees catchment is small relative to the rainfall it can receive in a single weather system. Saturated ground from earlier rainfall reduces infiltration; tidal locking at the estuary — where high tide blocks river outflow — can amplify upstream peaks. Defences are protection, not prevention.

A warmer atmosphere holds about 7% more water vapour for every 1°C of warming, so heavier rainfall events are becoming more common in the UK. The Met Office has linked record-breaking 2015 (Cumbria) and 2019–20 (Yorkshire, South Wales) floods to climate change. Future-proofing rivers therefore requires both grey infrastructure (defences) and green infrastructure (rewetted upland peat, replanted catchments, washlands) so the catchment as a whole holds more water before it reaches the channel.

Key Fact

The River Tees rises at Cross Fell (~893 m), flows 137 km through the High Force waterfall, meanders near Yarm, and enters the North Sea at Middlesbrough. Each course has been shaped by both physical and human change.

Why Glaciated Uplands Look the Way They Do

Around 18,000 years ago much of upland Britain lay under thick ice. Glaciers shaped the rock as they flowed, leaving today’s dramatic peaks, valleys and lakes. The UK’s glaciated uplands — the Lake District, Snowdonia, the Cairngorms, the Scottish Highlands — are relict landscapes: the ice itself has gone, but the landforms remain. Today’s climate continues to chip at them through freeze-thaw weathering and slope processes, but the dramatic shapes are inheritances from the last Ice Age.

How Glaciers Erode

Glaciers erode in two main ways. Plucking happens when meltwater at the base of the ice freezes around loose rock; as the glacier moves on, the rock is ripped out of the bedrock. Abrasion happens when the rocks frozen into the glacier’s base scrape across the bedrock below, leaving long parallel scratches called striations. The two processes work together: plucking takes blocks out, abrasion smooths what is left.

Key Fact

The four key erosional landforms are corries (armchair-shaped hollows), arêtes (knife-edge ridges), pyramidal peaks and U-shaped glacial troughs. They form when ice plucks and abrades hard upland rock.

Erosional Landforms

A corrie (also called a cwm in Wales or cirque in the Alps) is an armchair-shaped hollow on a mountain side. Snow accumulated in a sheltered hollow and compressed into ice; rotational movement of that ice plucked the back wall and abraded the floor; meltwater froze into cracks and prised out more rock. After the ice melted, a small lake (a tarn) often formed in the hollow. Red Tarn below Helvellyn is a textbook example. Where two corries developed back-to-back on opposite sides of a ridge, the rock between them was eroded down to a knife-edge arête — Striding Edge in the Lake District is a famous one. Where three or more corries surrounded a peak, the result is a pyramidal peak like Snowdon or the Matterhorn.

When a glacier flowed downhill it widened, deepened and straightened the valley it occupied. River-cut V-shaped valleys became U-shaped glacial troughs with steep sides and flat floors. The original interlocking spurs of the river were sheared off into truncated spurs. Tributary glaciers cut their valleys less deeply; once the ice melted, those valleys hung above the main trough as hanging valleys, often with a waterfall plunging from the rim. Llyn Idwal in Snowdonia and Wast Water in the Lake District sit in classic glacial troughs.

Depositional Landforms

Glaciers also dump material when they melt. Unsorted rocks and clay carried by ice are called moraine. Ground moraine blankets valley floors. Terminal moraine piles up at the snout of a glacier where ice melts as fast as it advances; it forms a curved ridge across the valley. Smaller landforms include drumlins — egg-shaped hills of moraine, with the steep end pointing in the direction the ice came from — and crag and tail, where harder rock protected softer rock from erosion behind it (Edinburgh Castle Rock and the Royal Mile is the classic example).

Sheep farming dominates UK uplands — hardy breeds like Herdwick graze where almost nothing else can. Conifer forestry plantations occupy steeper slopes, especially in the Lake District and Northumberland. Settlement sits in the valleys: stone-built villages like Grasmere and Beddgelert serve walkers and tourists. Reservoirs drown some valleys to supply distant cities — Thirlmere in the Lake District has fed Manchester since 1894. Each use changes the landscape, sometimes preserving its character (drystone walls, hedgerows), sometimes degrading it (overgrazing, soil erosion).

A Distinctive UK Glaciated Upland: The Lake District

The Lake District National Park covers 2,362 km2 in north-west England. Its slate, granite and volcanic rocks were folded by the Caledonian orogeny then sculpted by Ice Age glaciers into an iconic landscape: 16 main lakes filling glacial troughs, arêtes like Striding Edge and Sharp Edge, and pyramidal peaks like Helvellyn (950 m). Today over 18 million visitors a year bring £1.4 billion to the local economy but also create challenges: footpath erosion on Helvellyn cost the National Trust around £1.5 million to repair in the 2010s; second-home ownership pushes house prices beyond local wages; lake water quality has fallen as tourism intensifies.

Reservoirs supply clean water at scale and provide hydropower, but they drown valleys (and sometimes villages, as at Mardale Green under Haweswater). Wind farms generate renewable energy but change visual character — a major issue in protected upland landscapes. Tourism funds conservation and rural businesses but pressures footpaths, wildlife and housing. Conservation through National Park status protects landscapes but adds planning costs for residents who want to extend their homes. There is no neutral choice in upland development — every option carries trade-offs.

Key Fact

The Lake District contains pyramidal peaks (Helvellyn), arêtes (Striding Edge), corries with tarns (Red Tarn), glacial troughs (Wast Water) and ribbon lakes — all carved by ice 18,000 years ago and now under tourism pressure.

A Planet Spinning & Heating Unevenly

The Sun heats Earth’s surface unevenly. The equator receives roughly twice as much energy per square metre as the poles, because the Sun’s rays strike the equator almost vertically while striking the poles at a glancing angle. If nothing redistributed that heat, the tropics would be unbearably hot and the poles even colder. Instead, the atmosphere and oceans constantly transfer heat from low to high latitudes. The mechanism is global atmospheric circulation — six giant convection cells that drive everything from tropical storms to UK rainfall.

Three Cells in Each Hemisphere

Each hemisphere has three cells stacked between the equator and the pole. The Hadley cell runs from 0° to 30°. Warm equatorial air rises, cools, releases heavy rainfall (giving us tropical rainforests), then sinks at around 30° as dry air (giving us the Sahara, Kalahari and Australian deserts). The Ferrel cell runs from 30° to 60° — the UK sits inside this cell. Air rises again at around 60°, releasing rain over north-west Europe, then heads back down at the poles in the polar cell. Where cells meet, you find consistent climate signatures: rising air = wet, sinking air = dry.

Key Fact

Earth has six atmospheric cells — three in each hemisphere. Hot air rises at the equator and 60°; cool air sinks at 30° and the poles. Where air rises = wet; where air sinks = dry.

Ocean Currents: The Other Conveyor

Oceans transfer heat too. Surface currents driven by prevailing winds carry warm water polewards and cold water back to the equator. The Gulf Stream, part of the North Atlantic Drift, brings tropical-warm water northwards past the UK. Without it, Britain at 55°N would have a climate more like Canada at the same latitude — cold winters with sea ice. Instead, the Gulf Stream gives the UK its famous mild winters. Deep-ocean circulation, the ‘global conveyor belt’, takes thousands of years to complete one cycle but quietly redistributes heat across the planet.

The UK’s Climate Today

The UK has a temperate maritime climate. Average winter temperatures sit around 4–7°C across most of England; summers average 16–19°C. Annual rainfall ranges from over 4,000 mm in the Lake District to under 600 mm in East Anglia. Three factors create that variation. Latitude — northern Scotland is cooler than southern England because it receives less solar energy. Altitude — temperatures fall by around 1°C for every 100 m of elevation, so the Highlands are colder than the Lowlands. Distance from the sea — coastal areas have milder winters but cooler summers because oceans warm and cool slowly compared with land.

The UK’s prevailing south-westerly winds blow off the Atlantic carrying moist air. When that air hits western mountains (the Highlands, Snowdonia, the Lake District) it is forced to rise. Rising air cools, water vapour condenses and rain falls as relief rainfall. By the time the air descends on the eastern side of the country, it has lost most of its moisture — the rain-shadow effect. This is why Cumbria gets over 3,000 mm a year while Cambridgeshire receives less than 600 mm.

UK’s Position Inside the Cell

The UK sits at the boundary between the Ferrel and polar cells, where rising air encourages low-pressure weather systems known as depressions. These are the rotating storms that bring most of Britain’s rainfall and grey skies. They form along the polar front, where warm subtropical air meets cold polar air; the contrast in temperature and density forces air upwards, creating cloud and precipitation. UK rainfall is therefore mostly frontal, with depressions tracking eastwards across the Atlantic, often two or three a week in winter.

UK climate has shifted noticeably even within human history. The Medieval Warm Period (c.950–1250) was warm enough that vineyards grew across England as far north as Yorkshire. The Little Ice Age (c.1300–1850) was so cold that the Thames regularly froze and frost fairs were held on the ice in central London. Since 1850, average UK temperatures have risen by around 1°C, with the rate accelerating since 1980. Recent records: 40.3°C at Coningsby in July 2022 broke the all-time UK temperature record; six of the warmest UK years on record have happened since 2003.

Key Fact

The UK’s mild, wet climate is the product of: latitude (mid 50s °N); the Gulf Stream warming Atlantic air; and the prevailing south-westerly winds bringing moisture across western uplands.

A Storm With Many Names

Hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the western Pacific, cyclones in the Indian Ocean — the names differ but the storm is the same. A tropical cyclone is a deep low-pressure system with sustained winds above 119 km/h, an intense central eye and a spiral of rain bands hundreds of kilometres across. They are the most destructive natural hazards on the planet for low-latitude coasts. Where they form, when they peak and how a country copes are all controlled by physical geography — and by how much money the country has.

How They Form

Tropical cyclones form only between roughly 5° and 30° latitude (rarely on the equator itself). Four conditions must line up. First, sea-surface temperatures must reach 26.5°C or higher down to about 50 m depth, providing the energy. Second, warm ocean air must rise rapidly, cool, condense and release latent heat — powering the storm. Third, low vertical wind shear means upper and lower winds move at similar speeds, so the storm can stack and grow rather than tearing itself apart. Fourth, the Coriolis effect, caused by Earth’s rotation, twists the rising column into a spin (anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in the Southern). Once spinning, the storm pulls in more warm moist air from the surrounding ocean, intensifying further.

Key Fact

Tropical cyclones form between 5°–30° latitude when ocean temperatures reach 26.5°C, air rises rapidly, wind shear is low, and the Coriolis force gives the storm its spin.

Anatomy of a Storm

At the centre is the eye: 30–65 km wide, calm, with sinking air and clear skies. Around it is the eyewall, where the strongest winds and heaviest rainfall sit. Spiralling outwards are bands of cloud and rain that can stretch 600 km from the eye. Cyclones are rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale from Category 1 (119–153 km/h) to Category 5 (above 252 km/h), but wind speed alone hides the killer: storm surge, where low pressure and onshore winds push a wall of seawater inland, can drown coastal towns far worse than the wind.

Distribution & Frequency

Cyclones cluster in seven main basins. The North Atlantic and East Pacific seasons run June–November; the western North Pacific (typhoons) is active most of the year. The number of named storms varies year-on-year — a typical Atlantic season produces 14 named storms, of which 7 reach hurricane strength — but a clear trend is emerging: warmer oceans are producing fewer but more intense storms, and rapid intensification (a category jump in 24 hours) has become more common since 2000. Tracks are also shifting polewards as warmer water moves north and south.

In the eye, air is descending. Sinking air warms by compression, cloud evaporates and the surface is briefly clear. Survivors of direct hits often describe the eerie calm and even sunshine before the second eyewall arrives from the opposite direction. People who venture out during the eye thinking the storm is over are caught in the most dangerous winds when the back wall hits.

Hurricane Katrina, USA (2005) — Developed-Country Impact

Hurricane Katrina struck the US Gulf Coast on 29 August 2005 as a Category 3 storm with a 7-metre storm surge. Around 1,800 people died, most when the New Orleans levees failed and 80% of the city flooded. Damage reached $125 billion, the costliest US disaster on record. Despite the USA’s wealth, the response was widely criticised: poorer Black neighbourhoods of New Orleans had less car ownership and could not evacuate; the Superdome shelter became overcrowded with no air conditioning. Long-term, the city’s population fell from 484,000 (2000) to 343,000 (2010); levees were rebuilt to withstand a 100-year storm; insurance reform reshaped Gulf Coast property markets.

Cyclone Idai, Mozambique (2019) — Developing-Country Impact

Cyclone Idai struck the port city of Beira on 14 March 2019, sweeping across central Mozambique, Malawi and Zimbabwe. Over 1,300 people died and 3 million were displaced. Beira was 90% destroyed in a single night. Idai exposed how poverty multiplies a hazard: weakly built housing collapsed; warning systems reached too few people; only 2,500 hospital beds existed for an affected population of millions; cholera spread through floodwater, killing dozens more. International aid eventually arrived — the UK pledged £22 million — but distribution was slow because roads and bridges had been swept away. Mozambique’s GDP losses were estimated at $2 billion in a country where average annual income is $500.

Wealthier countries can afford preparation: hurricane-resistant building codes (Florida after Andrew), early-warning satellite systems, mass-evacuation transport networks, and well-equipped emergency services. Poorer countries depend more on international aid, charity NGOs and short-term rescue. Long-term, developed economies absorb the costs through insurance and reconstruction; developing economies often see GDP fall sharply for years, debt rise, and survivors push into informal urban settlements. The same Saffir-Simpson rating produces wildly different death tolls and recovery timelines depending on income.

Key Fact

Katrina (USA, 2005): 1,800 deaths, $125 billion damage, levee failure flooded 80% of New Orleans. Idai (Mozambique, 2019): over 1,300 deaths, $2 billion damage, Beira 90% destroyed, cholera outbreak followed.

A Slow-Burning Hazard

A drought is unlike a cyclone or earthquake: there is no single moment of impact. It begins quietly with low rainfall, deepens as soils dry out, and only becomes a crisis after months or years — by which time crops have failed, reservoirs have shrunk and food prices have surged. Drought is the most expensive natural hazard for global agriculture and one of the hardest to define, because what counts as ‘dry’ depends on what a place is used to. The Lake District seeing 600 mm of rain a year is normal; East Anglia seeing 600 mm is generous; the Sahel seeing 600 mm is a disaster only if it usually receives 800 mm.

Arid Environments vs Drought

An arid environment is one that is permanently dry — the Sahara, Atacama and central Australia receive less than 250 mm of rainfall a year as a baseline. Plants, animals and people adapt to that baseline. Drought is different: it is a temporary shortfall below normal rainfall, and it can hit even rainy places. The 2018 UK drought saw lawns brown, reservoirs drop and harvests fall by a quarter despite rainfall returning later that year. Confusing the two leads to weak exam answers — arid is a climate type, drought is an event.

Key Fact

Arid = permanently dry climate (under 250 mm rain/year). Drought = a temporary shortfall in rainfall below the local norm. Both can co-exist, but they are separate concepts.

Causes of Drought

Drought has three families of cause. Meteorological droughts begin when rainfall drops far below normal — typically because of shifts in the global circulation, sinking dry air at 30° latitude (where the Hadley cell descends), or warm-water/cool-water flips in the Pacific known as El Niño and La Niña. El Niño years drought-stress eastern Australia and southern Africa; La Niña tends to bring drought to the southern USA. Hydrological drought follows when rivers, reservoirs and groundwater stay low even after rain returns — aquifers can take decades to recharge. Human causes include over-extraction for agriculture (the Aral Sea has shrunk to 10% of its 1960 size from cotton irrigation), unsustainable dam-building upstream (the Mekong’s lower flow has been hit by Chinese dams), and large-scale deforestation that breaks the cycle of evaporation and rainfall (the Amazon basin sees longer dry seasons after forest loss).

The Hadley cell pushes dry sinking air down at 30° latitude, creating the world’s great deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Australian, Atacama). Areas just outside that band — the Sahel south of the Sahara, the south-west USA, north-east Brazil — have rainfall that is fragile to begin with and easily tipped into drought by El Niño or by climate change shifting the cell polewards. Climate change is making sinking-air zones drier and rising-air zones wetter, intensifying the natural pattern.

Why Droughts Are Hazardous

Droughts kill mainly through food and water shortages, not directly. Crop failure cuts farmer incomes and triggers food price spikes that hit the urban poor. Livestock die when grassland fails. Water rationing closes industries that need cooling water (power stations, paper mills). Wildfires become routine in tinder-dry vegetation: the 2019–20 Australian Black Summer fires, fuelled by the worst drought in centuries, killed 33 people, three billion animals and burnt 18 million hectares. Long droughts can drive permanent migration, as the Dust Bowl did in 1930s America when 2.5 million people abandoned the Great Plains.

Australia 2017–19 (Developed-Country Drought)

Eastern Australia experienced its driest period on record between 2017 and 2019. The Murray-Darling river system — which feeds 40% of Australia’s farms — ran near-dry; some towns reported reservoirs below 5% capacity. Sheep numbers crashed; wheat exports halved. The economic loss was estimated at AU$8 billion. Yet death tolls remained low because Australia is wealthy: water trucks were sent to towns; emergency loans propped up farms; psychological support services treated rural depression. The federal government released AU$7 billion in drought funding. The drought also triggered the Black Summer wildfires that followed in late 2019.

Ethiopia 2015–16 (Developing-Country Drought)

A severe El Niño triggered Ethiopia’s worst drought in 50 years. Around 10.2 million people needed food aid; over 400,000 children faced acute malnutrition; livestock losses ran into millions. The economic loss was harder to absorb than Australia’s: Ethiopia’s GDP per capita is about $1,000, agriculture employs 70% of the workforce, and many rural households had no insurance or savings. International appeals raised $700 million in emergency aid — less than half what the UN said was needed. Long-term responses included a Productive Safety Net Programme that pays the rural poor to build small dams, terraces and water-harvesting systems.

Top-down responses are large-scale and expensive: dams, desalination plants (Australia built six major plants after the Millennium Drought), inter-basin water transfers, drip irrigation subsidies, and crop insurance. Bottom-up responses are local and low-cost: rainwater harvesting from roofs into household tanks, drought-tolerant crop varieties (millet and sorghum instead of maize), terracing to slow runoff, and women’s cooperatives sharing wells. The most resilient countries combine both. Charity-led projects in Ethiopia (e.g. WaterAid’s sand dams) deliver water for under £30 per person reached.

Key Fact

Australia 2017–19: AU$8 billion loss, near-empty Murray-Darling, low death toll, federal aid programmes. Ethiopia 2015–16: 10.2 million needed food aid, 400,000 children malnourished, $700m international appeal.

A Living Planet, Mapped

From space, Earth’s land surface looks like a patchwork of greens, browns and yellows. Each colour reflects a biome — a continent-sized ecosystem shaped above all by climate. Tropical rainforests cluster around the equator. Hot deserts sit at 30° latitude where the Hadley cell descends. Temperate grasslands and deciduous forests fill the mid-latitudes. Boreal coniferous forests (the taiga) form a giant belt across northern Canada, Scandinavia and Russia. Tundra fringes the Arctic. The pattern is not random — it is the global circulation made visible.

What Climate & Local Factors Do

Two climate variables decide which biome forms where. Temperature controls how long a growing season is and which plants can survive winter; rainfall controls how lush vegetation can grow before water runs short. Plot any spot on Earth on a graph of mean temperature versus rainfall and you can predict its biome to within one band. Soil and altitude add finer detail. Tropical soils are deep but nutrient-poor (because heavy rain leaches them); temperate soils are deep and fertile; boreal soils are thin and acidic. Every 100 m of altitude is roughly equivalent to moving 100 km polewards — which is why mountainsides reproduce the global pattern in miniature, with rainforest below cloud forest below alpine meadow.

Key Fact

Climate (temperature and rainfall) sets the global pattern of biomes. Hot wet near the equator = rainforest. Hot dry at 30° = desert. Cool wet at 50–60° = boreal forest. Cold dry near the poles = tundra.

The Biosphere as a Resource

The biosphere is the global sum of all ecosystems — everywhere life exists. People depend on it for four main things. Food — over 7,000 plant species are eaten and 75% of global food comes from just 12 of them. Medicine — a quarter of modern drugs (including aspirin from willow and the cancer drug Taxol from Pacific yew) are biosphere-derived. Building materials — timber, bamboo, thatch, and indirectly limestone (from ancient sea creatures). Fuel — firewood still cooks the meals of 2.4 billion people; modern bioenergy adds 6% of UK electricity. The biosphere is also exploited commercially for energy (oil from former forests), water (irrigation extraction) and minerals (open-cast mining), each of which can damage the very ecosystems we depend on.

Plants take CO2 out of the atmosphere through photosynthesis and release oxygen; they also pump water back into the air through transpiration. Tropical forests alone store an estimated 250 gigatonnes of carbon — more than humans have emitted from fossil fuels since 1850. Soils store an additional 2,500 gigatonnes. Damage to ecosystems doesn’t just lose biodiversity; it releases stored carbon and reduces the planet’s ability to recycle gases. The biosphere is therefore a regulator as much as a resource.

UK Terrestrial Ecosystems

The UK is small but ecologically varied. Moorlands (about 12% of UK land area) cover upland Britain — peaty soils, heather, grouse and pipits dominate; the North York Moors and the Pennines are classic examples. Heathlands are lower-altitude open habitats on poor sandy soils — the New Forest and Dorset heaths support reptiles such as the smooth snake and Dartford warbler. Woodlands are mainly deciduous (oak, ash, beech) in the south and coniferous (Scots pine in the Caledonian forest) in northern Scotland. Wetlands — reed beds, fens, bogs — cover the Norfolk Broads, the Somerset Levels and Caerlaverock; they are migratory bird hotspots. Each ecosystem evolved with farming over millennia, so most is ‘semi-natural’ rather than truly wild.

UK Marine Ecosystems

UK seas are productive because cool Atlantic water mixes with shallow continental shelves. Cod, herring, mackerel and shellfish support a fishing industry worth around £1 billion at the dockside. Salt marshes on coasts like Morecambe Bay buffer storms and store carbon. Kelp forests off western Scotland host octopus, lobster and seal. But human pressure is severe: industrial trawling has cut North Sea cod stocks to a fraction of 1970s levels; sewage discharges have made many beaches unsafe; offshore oil and gas extraction has degraded seabed habitats. The 2009 Marine and Coastal Access Act created Marine Protected Areas to slow the damage; today, around 38% of UK seas have some level of protection on paper, though enforcement varies.

The Caledonian Forest in the Scottish Highlands is the UK’s only fragment of true boreal woodland — a relict of the post-Ice Age forest that once covered most of Scotland. The chalk grasslands of the South Downs (Sussex, Hampshire) are some of the richest grasslands in Europe, with up to 40 plant species per square metre. The Flow Country in northern Scotland is the world’s largest blanket bog, storing 400 million tonnes of carbon — designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024. Each is irreplaceable.

Key Fact

UK terrestrial ecosystems include moorland (Pennines), heathland (New Forest), woodland (Caledonian Forest, Sussex Weald) and wetland (Norfolk Broads). Marine ecosystems support a £1 billion fishing industry but face pressure from trawling, pollution and oil and gas extraction.
